questionText: Which of the following statements regarding Breadth First Search (BFS) and Depth First Search (DFS) on an undirected simple graph $G$ is/are TRUE?
options: A DFS tree of $G$ is a Shortest Path tree of $G$.
Every non-tree edge of $G$ with respect to a DFS tree is a forward/back edge.
If $(u, v)$ is a non-tree edge of $G$ with respect to a BFS tree, then the distances from the source vertex $s$ to $u$ and $v$ in the BFS tree are within $\pm 1$ of each other.
Both BFS and DFS can be used to find the connected components of $G$.
explanation:
Step-by-step Explanation:

• Statement (A) is FALSE: A BFS tree provides shortest path trees in unweighted graphs, but a DFS tree goes deep along each branch before backtracking, so it generally does not give the shortest path.

• Statement (B) is TRUE: For an undirected graph, a DFS tree produces only tree edges and back edges (forward and back edges are structurally identical in undirected graphs). Cross edges cannot exist.

• Statement (C) is TRUE: In a BFS tree of an undirected graph, non-tree edges can only exist between vertices residing in the same level or between adjacent levels. Therefore, $|d(s, u) - d(s, v)| \le 1$, meaning their distances from the source $s$ are within $\pm 1$ of each other.

• Statement (D) is TRUE: Both BFS and DFS visit every reachable vertex in a connected component, so running either algorithm iteratively on unvisited vertices can find all connected components of $G$.

Hence, statements (B), (C), and (D) are TRUE.
